blocks.text: **Hyperprolactinaemia** is a serum prolactin above the reference range. It is a common endocrine finding and usually shows itself as **hypogonadism**, **galactorrhoea** (milk production in someone who is not breastfeeding), or both. A **prolactinoma** is a pituitary adenoma whose cells secrete prolactin; it is the commonest _functioning_ pituitary tumour and the commonest pathological cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

blocks.title: Size classes of pituitary adenoma
rows: Usual type in pre-menopausal women; presents with endocrine symptoms
Men and post-menopausal women; mass effects (headache, visual fields)

blocks.title: Numbers quoted in quick-reference books
items: Prolactinomas make up roughly **40–50%** of pituitary adenomas (Step-Up: up to 40%; Pocket Medicine: 50%).
About **10%** of prolactinomas also secrete growth hormone (Pocket Medicine).
Pituitary adenomas are almost always benign and form about 10% of intracranial tumours.

blocks.text: **Macroprolactinoma ≠ macroprolactinaemia.** A macroprolactinoma is a prolactin-secreting tumour larger than 1 cm. Macroprolactinaemia is a lab phenomenon in which prolactin is bound to IgG, forming a large, biologically inactive complex: there is no tumour and nothing to treat.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: control and actions of prolactin

blocks.text: Prolactin is unusual among anterior pituitary hormones because its main hypothalamic control is **inhibitory**: dopamine reaching the pituitary through the portal vessels acts on **D2 receptors** and keeps prolactin release tonically suppressed. **TRH** stimulates prolactin, which matters clinically mainly in **primary hypothyroidism**.

blocks.title: What excess prolactin does
items: **Breast:** drives milk secretion, but does not make breast tissue grow.
**Hypothalamus:** reduces GnRH pulsatility, so LH and FSH fall.
**Gonads:** partly blocks LH action on ovary and testis, so hypogonadism occurs even with an intact pituitary–gonadal axis.
Result: low oestrogen or testosterone, giving amenorrhoea, infertility, low libido and, long term, osteoporosis.

blocks.title: Three mechanisms behind a high prolactin with a pituitary lesion
rows: Tumour cells secrete prolactin; level rises with tumour size
Any mass (e.g. non-functioning macroadenoma) compresses the infundibular stalk, cutting off dopamine
Loss of dopamine control means prolactin rises early while other hormones fall

blocks.text: Prolactin cells and GH cells share a lineage, so a prolactinoma occasionally co-secretes GH and causes acromegaly. In prolactinomas, the higher the prolactin, the bigger the tumour.
Men rarely develop galactorrhoea because prolactin cannot build breast tissue. It appears only when hypogonadism has already produced gynaecomastia.

blocks.note: Look at: dopamine inhibiting and TRH stimulating prolactin; prolactin suppressing GnRH and the gonadal action of LH while stimulating the breast.

blocks.title: Differential diagnosis (Davidson Box 18.58, with additions)
rows: Pregnancy, lactation, stress (e.g. after a seizure), sleep, coitus, exercise, nipple stimulation, a baby crying
Phenothiazine and butyrophenone antipsychotics; antidepressants (tricyclics, SSRIs); antiemetics metoclopramide and domperidone
Dopamine depleters (reserpine, methyldopa); oestrogens (combined pill); verapamil; cimetidine
Stalk disconnection (e.g. non-functioning macroadenoma), prolactinoma (usually micro), primary hypothyroidism, PCOS, macroprolactinaemia
GH/prolactin co-secreting tumour, hypothalamic disease, renal failure, liver failure / cirrhosis
Chest wall reflex (e.g. after herpes zoster), post-ictal state, idiopathic

blocks.title: Mechanisms worth knowing
items: **Primary hypothyroidism:** high TRH directly stimulates lactotrophs.
**Renal failure:** prolactin clearance is reduced.
**Stalk compression** by craniopharyngioma, meningioma or a non-secreting adenoma removes dopamine inhibition.
**Oestrogens** (combined pill, pregnancy) are a recognised cause, and oestrogen can also make a prolactinoma grow.

blocks.text: Most prolactinomas are **microadenomas**. Pituitary tumours, including prolactinomas, belong to **MEN 1**, which is why MEN 1 carriers have serum prolactin and calcium checked every year and pituitary/pancreatic MRI every 2 years.
Before labelling a prolactinoma, go through the "three Ps plus T": **pregnancy**, **pills** (drug history) and **physiological** stress, then **thyroid** (TSH). These are the commonest exam traps.

blocks.title: Presentation by patient group
rows: Oligo/amenorrhoea (secondary), anovulatory infertility, galactorrhoea (sometimes only on expression), low libido, dyspareunia, vaginal dryness
Usually micro: symptoms bring them early
Low libido, erectile dysfunction, infertility, shaving less often, lethargy; galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia uncommon
Often macro: early symptoms are dismissed
Hypogonadism is already physiological, so few endocrine symptoms
More often macro: they present late with mass effects

blocks.title: Mass effects of a macroprolactinoma
items: **Headache** from stretching of the diaphragma sellae.
**Visual field loss** from chiasmal compression: classically **bitemporal hemianopia** or upper quadrantanopia.
**Diplopia** if the tumour extends into the cavernous sinus (CN III, IV, VI), which is unusual.
**Hypopituitarism** from compression of the normal gland.

blocks.text: **Pituitary apoplexy** is bleeding into, or infarction of, a pituitary tumour. It causes sudden severe headache, local compression (visual loss, diplopia) and acute hypopituitarism. It needs immediate high-dose glucocorticoid, with urgent decompression if neurological deficit is severe.

Galactorrhoea does not prove hyperprolactinaemia: **normoprolactinaemic galactorrhoea** is common. Unilateral discharge in particular needs a breast examination to exclude malignancy or fibrocystic disease.

**Gynaecomastia:** First Aid lists it among the features of hyperprolactinaemia, but Davidson and Kumar explain it as a result of the associated **hypogonadism**, not a direct prolactin effect (Step-Up calls it uncommon). Follow Davidson.

blocks.note: Look at: the summary of pituitary disease (micro vs macroadenoma, mass effects, hormone excess and hypopituitarism).

blocks.title: Stepwise work-up
items: **1. Exclude pregnancy** in any woman who could be pregnant.
**2. Serum prolactin:** prolactin is not pulsatile, so one random sample is enough if the venepuncture was not stressful.
**3. Review drugs** and repeat prolactin after stopping culprits where safe.
**4. T4 and TSH** to exclude primary hypothyroidism; check gonadal function and renal function.
**5. Exclude macroprolactin** (PEG precipitation or gel filtration) if the assay cross-reacts.
**6. Pituitary MRI** (or CT) if prolactin stays high without another explanation.
**7. With a macroadenoma:** visual fields and full anterior pituitary function.

blocks.title: Interpreting prolactin (Davidson; non-pregnant, non-lactating)
rows: Stress or drugs; repeat the test
Highly suggestive of macroprolactinoma (can exceed 100 000 mIU/L)

blocks.text: With a pituitary mass on MRI, the prolactin level separates the two diagnoses: a **very high** level means prolactinoma, while a **modest** rise with a large tumour suggests a non-functioning adenoma causing stalk disconnection.

**Hook effect:** a giant prolactinoma can produce so much prolactin that some assays read falsely low. If a large tumour has only a modest prolactin, ask the lab to repeat on **serially diluted** serum.
Always measure prolactin **before emergency surgery** on a sellar mass. A level above 5000 mIU/L implies a macroprolactinoma that should shrink on a dopamine agonist, making surgery unnecessary.
Up to 10% of healthy middle-aged adults have an MRI pituitary "abnormality". Image only after a clear biochemical abnormality, or with clinical features of a tumour.

**Single versus repeat sample:** Davidson accepts one random prolactin if the patient was not stressed, repeating only mild rises (500–1000 mIU/L). Kumar advises confirming every raised value with a repeat. Follow Davidson.

blocks.note: Look at: the range of serum prolactin for each common cause (stress, pregnancy, drugs, hypothyroidism, renal failure, stalk compression, micro- and macroprolactinoma), with macroprolactinoma reaching the highest levels.

blocks.text: Treat the cause first: stop offending drugs where possible and give **levothyroxine** for primary hypothyroidism. If an antipsychotic (dopamine antagonist) is the cause and must continue, a dopamine agonist is **contraindicated**; give sex-steroid replacement for the hypogonadism instead. For a prolactinoma, a **dopamine agonist is first line** (Box 18.57), and it usually shrinks even macroadenomas.

blocks.title: Dopamine agonists (Davidson Box 18.59)
rows: Long-acting; fewer ergot side-effects; Kumar: drug of choice; Step-Up: often chosen first
Limited pregnancy data; valve fibrosis at Parkinson doses
Longest experience; short half-life; preferred when pregnancy is planned
Nausea, headache, postural hypotension, constipation; frequent dosing harms adherence
Non-ergot; for patients intolerant of the others

blocks.title: Using them
items: Start low and titrate slowly to limit nausea and postural hypotension, especially with bromocriptine.
Visual field defects can improve **within days**; tumour shrinkage takes **months**.
Treat every macroprolactinoma and troublesome galactorrhoea. A post-menopausal woman with a microprolactinoma may need no treatment.
An asymptomatic microadenoma can be followed with MRI; only 10–20% of microadenomas keep growing.
Fertility can return quickly, so contraception is needed if pregnancy is not wanted.

blocks.title: Stopping treatment
items: **Microadenoma:** a withdrawal trial after a few years (Kumar: 2–3 years; Step-Up: about 2 years) often succeeds.
**Macroadenoma:** most recur, so withdraw only after curative surgery or radiotherapy and under close supervision.

blocks.text: Ergot agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline) act on **5-HT2B** receptors and can cause fibrosis, especially **tricuspid regurgitation**, at the high doses used in Parkinson’s disease. Routine echo screening is usually unnecessary at prolactinoma doses, but consider periodic echo or a non-ergot agent (quinagolide) for long-term use. Dopamine agonists can also cause **impulse-control disorders** such as gambling.

blocks.note: Look at: macroprolactinoma compressing the optic chiasm, then marked shrinkage with the chiasm freed after dopamine agonist therapy.

blocks.title: Second-line options
rows: Macroprolactinoma that shrinks too little (sometimes because it is cystic); drug intolerance; persisting visual loss
Cures about 80% of microadenomas, with possible recurrence; much lower cure rate for macroadenomas, which usually still need a dopamine agonist
Some macroadenomas, to stop regrowth when the agonist is withdrawn; failure of drugs and surgery
Acts over months to years, so useless for urgent cases; fractionated RT causes hypopituitarism in 50–70% within 10 years, so annual pituitary testing is needed

blocks.text: Compressed visual pathways are **urgent**: recovery is less likely the longer the defect has lasted, and full recovery is unlikely after **4 months**. For a prolactinoma, urgent treatment means a dopamine agonist, not surgery.

blocks.title: Pregnancy (Davidson)
rows: Stop the dopamine agonist as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Oestrogen can make it grow quickly: continue the agonist and monitor prolactin and visual fields
Report headache or visual disturbance promptly

blocks.text: **Books differ on pregnancy.** Davidson continues the agonist through pregnancy for a macroprolactinoma. Kumar describes agonists as traditionally stopped after conception (particularly for microprolactinomas) and restarted if the tumour grows. The Washington Manual advises delaying pregnancy until a macroprolactinoma is resected or markedly shrunk (15–35% enlarge symptomatically). For the exam, follow Davidson.
Bromocriptine is the agonist preferred when pregnancy is planned because it has the longest safety record. Pregnancy data on cabergoline and quinagolide are more limited.

blocks.note: Look at: a macroprolactinoma before treatment and after 2 years of cabergoline, showing marked shrinkage.

cards.front: Size cut-off between micro- and macroprolactinoma?
cards.back: 10 mm: micro < 10 mm, macro > 10 mm (> 1 cm)
Prolactin bound to IgG: a large, biologically inactive complex that causes spurious hyperprolactinaemia; not a tumour
Tonic **inhibition by dopamine** acting on pituitary D2 receptors; TRH stimulates

cards.front: How does prolactin excess cause hypogonadism?
cards.back: Reduces GnRH pulsatility (low LH/FSH) and partly blocks LH action on the gonads
A mass compresses the pituitary stalk, so dopamine cannot reach the lactotrophs and prolactin rises modestly

cards.front: Why does primary hypothyroidism raise prolactin?
Why do men and post-menopausal women present with larger prolactinomas?
cards.back: Hypogonadal symptoms are missed or dismissed, so they present late with mass effects

cards.front: Classic visual field defect of a macroprolactinoma?
cards.back: Bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression) or upper quadrantanopia

cards.front: First test in a woman of reproductive age with high prolactin?
Prolactin level highly suggestive of macroprolactinoma (Davidson)?
Hook effect: what is it and how do you exclude it?
cards.back: Extremely high prolactin gives a falsely low assay result; repeat on serially diluted serum

cards.front: First-line treatment of a prolactinoma, even a macroadenoma with visual loss?
Cardiac risk of ergot dopamine agonists?
cards.back: Valvular fibrosis (especially tricuspid regurgitation) via 5-HT2B receptors, mainly at Parkinson doses

cards.front: Dopamine agonist in pregnancy: micro vs macroprolactinoma (Davidson)?
cards.back: Micro: stop once pregnancy is confirmed. Macro: continue, and monitor prolactin and visual fields

cards.front: Main long-term complication of pituitary radiotherapy?
cards.back: Hypopituitarism (50–70% within 10 years), so pituitary function is tested yearly

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has secondary amenorrhoea. Serum prolactin is raised, and pituitary MRI shows a 6 mm lesion.
questions.leadIn: Which term best describes the lesion?
questions.explanation: A prolactin-secreting adenoma **under 10 mm** is a **microprolactinoma**, the usual type in pre-menopausal women because symptoms bring them to medical attention early.
whyNot: Macroprolactinomas are larger than 10 mm.
Macroprolactinaemia is IgG-bound prolactin, a lab phenomenon with no tumour.
Craniopharyngioma is usually a suprasellar mass and does not explain a small intrasellar lesion with high prolactin.
Kumar reserves "mesoadenoma" for tumours of about 10 mm, not 6 mm.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with regular periods and no galactorrhoea has a prolactin of 1400 mIU/L on a routine screen. After polyethylene glycol precipitation, her prolactin is within the reference range. Pituitary MRI is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Prolactin bound to IgG (**macroprolactin**) is detected by some assays but cannot reach tissue receptors. PEG precipitation removes it, and the remaining **monomeric prolactin is normal**, which fits an asymptomatic patient with normal imaging.
whyNot: A microprolactinoma raises monomeric prolactin, which would stay high after PEG precipitation.
Stalk disconnection needs a mass compressing the stalk, and her MRI is normal.
The hook effect gives a falsely low result with a huge tumour, not a falsely high one.
Hypothyroidism raises true monomeric prolactin, which PEG would not remove.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to explain why removing the pituitary stalk from its hypothalamic connections raises prolactin while other anterior pituitary hormones fall.
questions.leadIn: Which hypothalamic factor normally restrains prolactin release?
questions.explanation: Prolactin is under **tonic dopamine inhibition** through D2 receptors. Cut the stalk and dopamine no longer arrives, so prolactin rises (disconnection hyperprolactinaemia) while hormones that need hypothalamic stimulation fall.
whyNot: TRH stimulates prolactin rather than inhibiting it.
GnRH controls LH and FSH; prolactin suppresses GnRH, not the other way round.
Somatostatin chiefly inhibits GH and TSH.
Vasopressin is a posterior pituitary hormone with no main role in prolactin control.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with a prolactinoma asks why her periods stopped.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism?
options: Prolactin suppresses GnRH pulsatility and blunts LH action on the ovary
questions.explanation: High prolactin **reduces hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility**, so LH and FSH fall, and it also partly **blocks LH action** at the gonad. This causes hypogonadism even when the pituitary is otherwise intact, as in a microadenoma.
whyNot: Follicles are not destroyed; ovulation recovers when prolactin falls.
Compression causes hypogonadism mainly with large tumours, but a microprolactinoma acts through hormonal suppression.
SHBG is not the mechanism described.
Adrenal androgen excess is not the explanation for the amenorrhoea.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia has galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea after starting a new medication. Pregnancy test is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Butyrophenone and phenothiazine antipsychotics are **dopamine antagonists**, so they remove the tonic dopamine brake on prolactin. Haloperidol is a classic cause.
whyNot: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist and lowers prolactin.
Levothyroxine lowers prolactin in hypothyroidism by reducing TRH.
Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist used to treat hyperprolactinaemia.
Lithium is not a dopamine antagonist and is not a classic cause.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain, constipation, oligomenorrhoea and a prolactin of 1200 mIU/L. TSH is markedly raised and free T4 is low.
questions.leadIn: What is the best next step?
questions.explanation: In **primary hypothyroidism**, high TRH stimulates prolactin. Treating the cause with **levothyroxine** should bring prolactin down, so recheck before considering imaging or dopamine agonists.
whyNot: A dopamine agonist treats the symptom but leaves the cause untreated.
Imaging is premature until the reversible cause is treated; MRI abnormalities are common in healthy people.
There is no evidence of a tumour needing surgery.
The clinical and thyroid picture explains true hyperprolactinaemia; macroprolactin testing is not the priority.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has had headaches for a year and recently bumped into door frames on both sides. He admits his libido has been low for several years.
questions.leadIn: Which visual field defect is most likely?
questions.explanation: Men often present late, with a macroprolactinoma that has grown upward to press on the **optic chiasm**. Compression of the crossing nasal fibres causes **bitemporal hemianopia**, so he misses objects on both sides.
whyNot: A unilateral central scotoma reflects optic nerve compression and would not cause bilateral lateral misses.
A homonymous defect comes from the optic tract or beyond, which is less typical.
Binasal loss is not the pattern of chiasmal compression.
Glaucoma does not explain low libido or headache.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a 2-year history of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction. He has no breast tissue enlargement.
questions.leadIn: Which feature is least likely to be present if his cause is hyperprolactinaemia?
questions.explanation: Prolactin drives milk secretion but **not breast growth**, so galactorrhoea in men is rare and occurs only when hypogonadism has already caused gynaecomastia. He has no breast enlargement, so galactorrhoea is unlikely.
whyNot: Reduced shaving is a classic hypogonadal symptom in men with high prolactin.
Lethargy is commonly reported.
Low testosterone follows GnRH suppression.
Infertility results from the hypogonadism.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with galactorrhoea and 4 months without a period.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation should be performed first?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy is the commonest cause of both amenorrhoea and a high prolactin, so it must be **excluded first** in any woman who could be pregnant, before other tests.
whyNot: Prolactin is needed, but a raised value is uninterpretable until pregnancy is excluded.
Imaging comes after biochemistry and exclusion of secondary causes.
TSH is part of the work-up but follows a pregnancy test.
Visual fields matter with a macroadenoma; they are not the first step.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has a 3.5 cm pituitary mass reaching the chiasm. His serum prolactin is reported as only modestly raised.
questions.leadIn: What should be done to interpret the prolactin result correctly?
options: Repeat the assay on serially diluted serum
Measure prolactin after a TRH test
questions.explanation: A giant prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low reading (**hook effect**). **Serial dilution** reveals the true, very high value and separates a prolactinoma from a non-functioning tumour causing stalk disconnection.
whyNot: IGF-1 screens for acromegaly; it does not correct the prolactin result.
PEG precipitation detects macroprolactin, a cause of falsely high results.
A TRH test does not overcome assay saturation.
Cortisol is part of assessing hypopituitarism, but it does not fix the prolactin interpretation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a 7 mm prolactinoma with amenorrhoea and troublesome galactorrhoea. She is not planning pregnancy.
questions.leadIn: What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists are **first line** for prolactinomas. Cabergoline is long-acting, taken twice weekly and better tolerated than bromocriptine.
whyNot: Surgery is second line for prolactinomas.
Radiotherapy is second line and slow, and it causes hypopituitarism.
Sex steroids replace oestrogen but do nothing for galactorrhoea or the tumour.
Somatostatin analogues treat acromegaly, not prolactinoma.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia, stable on risperidone, has low libido and a prolactin of 2100 mIU/L. MRI pituitary is normal, and his psychiatrist advises against changing the antipsychotic.
questions.leadIn: Which approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: When a needed **dopamine antagonist** causes hyperprolactinaemia, a dopamine agonist is **contraindicated** because it can undo the antipsychotic effect. Treat the gonadal deficiency with **sex-steroid replacement**.
whyNot: A dopamine agonist opposes the antipsychotic and could cause a psychotic relapse.
Cabergoline has the same problem as any dopamine agonist here.
The MRI is normal; there is nothing to operate on.
Radiotherapy has no role in drug-induced hyperprolactinaemia.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with a 5 mm microprolactinoma conceived 4 weeks after starting bromocriptine. Pregnancy is now confirmed.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what should be done with her dopamine agonist?
questions.explanation: Microadenomas rarely enlarge in pregnancy, so Davidson advises **stopping the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed**, with prompt reporting of headache or visual change.
whyNot: Continuing is the Davidson plan for a **macro**prolactinoma, which may grow under oestrogen.
Cabergoline has more limited pregnancy safety data, and no agonist is needed here.
There is no indication to increase treatment.
Radiotherapy has no place in pregnancy for a microadenoma.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with a cystic macroprolactinoma has persisting visual field loss despite 6 months of maximum-dose cabergoline.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Surgery is needed mainly when a macroprolactinoma **fails to shrink enough** on a dopamine agonist, often because of a **cystic** component, or when visual defects persist.
whyNot: Switching agonist is unlikely to shrink a cystic tumour, and vision cannot wait.
Stopping treatment would let the tumour regrow and vision worsen.
Octreotide treats acromegaly, not prolactinoma.
Radiotherapy takes months to years and cannot relieve urgent chiasmal compression.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 2.8 cm pituitary mass compressing the chiasm, found on CT after a fall. Neurosurgery is planned for the next morning.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most important before surgery?
questions.explanation: If prolactin exceeds **5000 mIU/L**, the mass is probably a macroprolactinoma that will shrink on a **dopamine agonist**, making surgery unnecessary. Prolactin should always be checked before emergency sellar surgery.
whyNot: IGF-1 screens for acromegaly but would not change the urgent plan the way prolactin can.
Screening for Cushing’s does not decide whether surgery is avoidable.
Calcium is relevant to MEN 1 but not to the surgical decision.
Metanephrines are for phaeochromocytoma, not a sellar mass.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with irregular periods, hirsutism, acne and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound has a prolactin of 850 mIU/L. Pregnancy test and TSH are normal.
questions.leadIn: Which cause best explains her prolactin?
questions.explanation: **PCOS** is a common pathological cause of a mild prolactin rise, and her hirsutism, acne and ovarian findings fit it. A level of 500–1000 mIU/L should still be repeated to rule out stress.
whyNot: A macroprolactinoma usually gives levels above 5000 mIU/L.
Stalk disconnection needs a mass on imaging, and there is nothing to suggest one.
Nothing suggests renal failure.
Co-secreting tumours are uncommon and cause acromegalic features.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has taken cabergoline at high dose for many years for a macroprolactinoma. A new pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge is heard.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism links his murmur to the drug?
questions.explanation: Ergot-derived agonists such as cabergoline stimulate **5-HT2B** receptors and can cause **valve fibrosis**, classically **tricuspid regurgitation** (a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge), especially at high cumulative doses.
whyNot: Cabergoline is a D2 agonist, not an antagonist, and does not cause cardiomyopathy this way.
Prolactin does not cause endocarditis.
There is no evidence of hypothyroidism, and an effusion does not cause a murmur.
Hypogonadism is not linked to aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with acromegaly has a raised prolactin as well as a high IGF-1.
questions.leadIn: Why might a pituitary tumour secrete both GH and prolactin?
options: Somatotrophs and lactotrophs share a common cell lineage
Both hormones are made in the posterior pituitary
questions.explanation: Prolactin-secreting and GH-secreting cells derive from a **common lineage**, so mixed tumours occur. Step-Up notes that about 30% of patients with acromegaly have hyperprolactinaemia.
whyNot: GH does not directly stimulate lactotrophs in this way.
IGF-1 does not block hypothalamic dopamine.
The hormones are separate gene products.
Both are anterior pituitary hormones.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man has a 2.5 cm sellar mass reaching the chiasm. His prolactin is 1800 mIU/L, and repeat measurement on diluted serum gives the same value. IGF-1 and cortisol tests are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A macroprolactinoma this large would usually give a prolactin **above 5000 mIU/L**, and dilution has excluded the hook effect. A **modest** rise with a large mass points to **stalk compression** by a non-functioning adenoma. This matters because such tumours do not shrink on dopamine agonists and need surgery.
whyNot: Macroprolactinomas produce prolactin roughly in proportion to size, so 1800 mIU/L is too low once the hook effect is excluded.
The tumour is 2.5 cm, so it is not a microadenoma.
Macroprolactinaemia does not produce a sellar mass.
Normal IGF-1 argues against acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden, severe headache, vomiting and double vision. He is drowsy, and his blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: This is **pituitary apoplexy**: bleeding or infarction in the tumour causing acute compression and **acute hypopituitarism**. Cortisol deficiency is life-threatening, so give **high-dose glucocorticoid immediately**, and consider urgent decompression for severe deficits.
whyNot: A dopamine agonist works too slowly and does not treat adrenal crisis.
Thyroid hormone does not treat the life-threatening cortisol deficiency, and giving it before glucocorticoid can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Radiotherapy has no role in the acute event.
Mannitol does not address the acute cortisol deficiency.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old post-menopausal woman has an incidental 6 mm prolactinoma. She has no galactorrhoea, headache or visual symptoms.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: After the menopause, **hypogonadism is physiological** and a microadenoma rarely grows, so a microprolactinoma needs treatment only if galactorrhoea is troublesome.
whyNot: There is nothing to treat; prolactin suppression would bring no benefit.
Surgery is not indicated for an asymptomatic microadenoma.
Radiotherapy risks hypopituitarism with no benefit.
HRT is not needed to treat the prolactinoma.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on haemodialysis has a mildly raised prolactin. She takes no regular medication other than phosphate binders.
questions.leadIn: What is the main reason for her raised prolactin?
questions.explanation: **Renal failure** raises prolactin mainly because the kidneys clear less of it.
whyNot: Her thyroid status is not given; renal failure itself explains the result.
Nothing suggests a sellar mass.
She is post-menopausal and takes no oestrogen.
She has never been on a dopamine agonist.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had secondary amenorrhoea for 8 months and expressible galactorrhoea. Pregnancy test is negative, she takes no medication, and TSH is normal. Prolactin is 3200 mIU/L on two samples.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Step 1: pregnancy is excluded. Step 2: there are no drug causes. Step 3: TSH is normal, so primary hypothyroidism is excluded. Step 4: the prolactin is persistently raised in the **1000–5000 mIU/L** band, which fits a microprolactinoma or stalk disconnection. Step 5: a persistently high, unexplained prolactin is the indication for **pituitary MRI**.
whyNot: Ultrasound may show PCOS, but it cannot exclude a pituitary lesion.
Delay is not appropriate; the cause must be found.
Synacthen tests adrenal reserve and is not the next step for a probable microadenoma.
Imaging should define the lesion before treatment.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has headache and bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 3 cm sellar mass compressing the chiasm, and serum prolactin is 48 000 mIU/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the best initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Step 1: prolactin is far above 5000 mIU/L, so this is a **macroprolactinoma**. Step 2: prolactinomas respond to dopamine agonists, which usually shrink even large tumours. Step 3: visual fields often improve **within days**, so medical therapy is the urgent treatment and surgery is avoided. Step 4: monitor visual fields and repeat MRI; surgery is for failure or intolerance.
whyNot: Surgery is second line and has a low cure rate for macroprolactinomas.
Radiotherapy acts over months to years.
Hydrocortisone is given for adrenal insufficiency, but does not treat the tumour.
Quinagolide is a dopamine agonist for those intolerant of others; surgery is not first.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a 2 cm macroprolactinoma has shrunk well on cabergoline and now wants to conceive. She asks what will happen to her treatment if she becomes pregnant.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, what is the correct advice?
options: Continue the dopamine agonist in pregnancy, with prolactin and visual field monitoring
Stop the dopamine agonist at conception and never restart
questions.explanation: Step 1: decide the size. A 2 cm tumour is a **macro**prolactinoma. Step 2: oestrogen in pregnancy can make it **grow quickly**. Step 3: Davidson therefore advises **continuing** the agonist, monitoring prolactin and visual fields, and reporting headache or visual change promptly. (Kumar and Washington are more cautious; follow Davidson for the exam.)
whyNot: Stopping is the Davidson plan for **micro**adenomas only.
Radiotherapy is not first-line and causes hypopituitarism.
Pregnancy is not forbidden; it needs planning and monitoring.
Oestrogen would stimulate the tumour.

questions.theme: Causes of a raised serum prolactin
questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most likely cause of the raised prolactin from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Stalk disconnection by a non-functioning adenoma
Chest wall reflex after herpes zoster

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has 3 months of amenorrhoea, nausea and breast tenderness. Prolactin is 1600 mIU/L.
items.explanation: Pregnancy is the commonest cause of amenorrhoea with a raised prolactin, and nausea and breast tenderness support it. A pregnancy test comes first.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with gastroparesis has been taking a prokinetic antiemetic before meals for 3 months and now notices reduced libido. Prolactin is 1900 mIU/L.
items.explanation: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist used as a prokinetic, and it raises prolactin.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is seen 30 minutes after a generalised tonic–clonic seizure. A prolactin taken in the emergency department is mildly raised.
items.explanation: The stress of a seizure transiently raises prolactin (post-ictal state).

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has bitemporal hemianopia and a 3 cm sellar mass. Prolactin is 2200 mIU/L, unchanged on dilution. Cabergoline normalises prolactin, but the tumour does not shrink.
items.explanation: Two steps: a large mass with only a modest prolactin, after the hook effect is excluded, suggests stalk compression; a true macroprolactinoma would usually shrink on a dopamine agonist, so failure to shrink supports a non-functioning adenoma.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has a painful vesicular rash in a band around her right chest, which healed 2 months ago with persistent neuralgia. She now has galactorrhoea, normal TSH and normal pituitary MRI.
items.explanation: Stimulation of the chest wall nerves (for example after herpes zoster) is a rare reflex cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

questions.leadIn: For each patient below, choose the most appropriate management from the list above. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Stop the offending drug and recheck prolactin

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with a microprolactinoma and anovulatory infertility wants to conceive within the next year. She has not yet started treatment.
items.explanation: Bromocriptine has the longest safety record when pregnancy is planned, and Davidson notes its use in infertility. Cabergoline has more limited pregnancy data.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has taken cabergoline for a prolactinoma, but echocardiography now shows new tricuspid regurgitation. He still needs a dopamine agonist.
items.explanation: Quinagolide is a non-ergot agonist, so it avoids 5-HT2B-mediated valve fibrosis and suits patients who need long-term therapy.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 4 mm microprolactinoma, treated with cabergoline, has a positive pregnancy test.
items.explanation: Davidson advises stopping the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed in a microadenoma, because significant growth is unlikely.

items.stem: A 39-year-old man has a macroprolactinoma that has not been controlled despite surgery and maximum tolerated dopamine agonist therapy. He wants to stop medication long term.
items.explanation: Radiotherapy is reserved for failure of medical and surgical therapy and to prevent regrowth when agonists are withdrawn. It works slowly and causes hypopituitarism, so annual pituitary tests are needed.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman has a prolactin of 720 mIU/L on a sample taken after she fainted during venepuncture. She is well, with regular periods, and takes no medication.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the prolactin under calm conditions
questions.explanation: A level of **500–1000 mIU/L** is usually due to **stress** or drugs, and her sample was taken under obvious stress. Davidson advises a **repeat** before further work-up.
whyNot: Imaging before confirming a true rise risks finding an incidental "abnormality".
There is no confirmed hyperprolactinaemia to treat.
Visual fields are needed for a macroadenoma, not for a single mild rise.
Nothing suggests acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman starts bromocriptine for a microprolactinoma and stops it after 2 days because of dizziness on standing and nausea.
questions.leadIn: What would most reduce these side-effects if she restarts?
options: Start at a low dose with food and titrate slowly
Take the full dose at once to build tolerance
Take it on an empty stomach in the morning
questions.explanation: Bromocriptine causes ergot-type effects (**nausea, postural hypotension**). Starting at a **low dose, with food** (often at bedtime), and increasing slowly reduces them. Tolerance develops over time.
whyNot: A large initial dose makes postural hypotension worse.
Domperidone is a dopamine antagonist that raises prolactin.
Octreotide does not treat prolactinoma.
An empty stomach worsens nausea.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had oligomenorrhoea for 2 years and has a prolactin of 3000 mIU/L due to a microprolactinoma. She asks about the long-term risk if she is not treated.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is she most at risk of?
questions.explanation: Prolonged **oestrogen deficiency** from prolactin-induced hypogonadism reduces bone density, so **osteoporosis** is the key long-term risk and one reason to treat.
whyNot: Kumar mentions only an epidemiological association, not an established complication.
Prolactinomas do not secrete ACTH.
Diabetes insipidus is a posterior pituitary/hypothalamic disorder, rare with prolactinoma.
Hypercalcaemia would raise suspicion of MEN 1, but it is not a complication of prolactinoma.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has a 5 mm prolactinoma. Her mother had parathyroidectomy for hypercalcaemia, and her brother had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour.
questions.leadIn: Which test is most appropriate for her?
questions.explanation: Prolactinoma with a family history of **hyperparathyroidism** and a **pancreatic tumour** suggests **MEN 1**. Serum calcium (with PTH) screens for the primary hyperparathyroidism of MEN 1; MEN 1 carriers have calcium and prolactin checked every year.
whyNot: Calcitonin screens for medullary thyroid cancer in MEN 2.
Metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, a MEN 2 feature.
5-HIAA is for carcinoid syndrome.
IGF-1 assesses GH excess, which is not the most useful test here.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man has a macroprolactinoma that has shrunk well after 3 years of cabergoline, with normal prolactin. He has not had surgery or radiotherapy. He asks to stop the drug.
questions.leadIn: What is the best advice?
options: Most macroprolactinomas recur, so continue unless curative surgery or radiotherapy has been done
Stop now and repeat MRI in 5 years
Halve the dose and stop at 4 years
questions.explanation: Davidson allows withdrawal of a dopamine agonist in a **macroadenoma** only after **curative surgery or radiotherapy** and under close supervision, because **most recur**. Withdrawal trials suit **micro**adenomas.
whyNot: Recurrence after stopping is the rule in macroadenomas.
Stopping without supervision risks regrowth and visual loss.
Radiotherapy is not needed for a well-controlled tumour.
An arbitrary taper has no supporting basis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man had fractionated pituitary radiotherapy 6 years ago for a macroprolactinoma. He now has fatigue, cold intolerance and low libido.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Fractionated pituitary radiotherapy causes **progressive hypopituitarism** in **50–70% within 10 years**, so annual pituitary function testing is obligatory. His symptoms fit central hypothyroidism and hypogonadism.
whyNot: The hook effect is an assay artefact and does not explain the symptoms.
Valvulopathy would cause cardiac signs, not this pattern.
Radiotherapy to the sellar region causes loss of anterior pituitary hormones, so any hypothyroidism here would be secondary (TSH deficiency), not primary.
Several hormone-deficiency symptoms after radiotherapy should not be dismissed.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with galactorrhoea has a prolactin of 1500 mIU/L. Pregnancy test and TSH are normal. She takes citalopram, which cannot easily be stopped.
questions.leadIn: Which statement about further work-up is most accurate?
options: Pituitary MRI is indicated if prolactin stays raised, because the drug cannot be withdrawn to show it is the cause
SSRIs never raise prolactin, so image immediately
Hyperprolactinaemia is excluded because galactorrhoea is often normoprolactinaemic
Measure GH after a glucose load
questions.explanation: SSRIs can raise prolactin, but the usual way to prove a drug cause is to show prolactin falls after withdrawal. When the drug cannot be stopped and prolactin stays raised, that proof is unavailable, so **pituitary imaging** is needed to exclude a tumour.
whyNot: SSRIs are a recognised cause of hyperprolactinaemia.
Treatment should not begin without establishing the cause.
Her prolactin is raised, so this is not normoprolactinaemic galactorrhoea.
A glucose suppression test is for acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 2.2 cm prolactinoma with superior extension and a mild bitemporal field defect. He starts cabergoline.
questions.leadIn: Which response pattern is expected?
options: Visual fields may improve within days, while tumour shrinkage occurs over months
Visual fields cannot improve without surgery
The tumour shrinks in days, but fields take years
Prolactin falls, but the tumour never shrinks
questions.explanation: Dopamine agonists lower prolactin and **shrink macroprolactinomas over months**, but **visual fields can improve within days**. Washington reports normalised prolactin, shrinkage and better fields in about 90%; visual fields are rechecked at 4–6 weeks and MRI at 3–6 months.
whyNot: Most patients improve with medical therapy alone.
This reverses the real time course.
Prolactinomas usually shrink; failure to shrink suggests a cystic tumour or non-prolactinoma.
Shrinkage is visible within months.

ospe.identify: MRI: pituitary macroadenoma (prolactinoma) lifting and compressing the optic chiasm, then shrinkage with the chiasm decompressed after dopamine agonist therapy, showing that medical treatment is first line even for large tumours.
MRI before and after 2 years of cabergoline: a macroprolactinoma (arrowed) with marked shrinkage on treatment.

Pituitary disease summary: micro- versus macroadenoma on MRI, local complications (headache, visual field defect, diplopia, apoplexy), hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, hypogonadism) and hypopituitarism.
